Two Radii for Mean Shift

cv.pyrMeanShiftFiltering takes two radii: sp, how far away in the image a pixel may be and still count, and sr, how different in color. Every combination below was run by OpenCV on the notebook's photo, and timed.

Radii

Color space

The function works on whatever three channels it is given. An 8-bit L*u*v* image and a BGR image both hold values from 0 to 255, but a distance of 40 does not mean the same change of color in both, so the same sr merges different amounts.

Measured

time on one laptop-
regions of 100+ pixels-

Regions are connected areas of almost equal color (a flood fill with tolerance 1 per channel), the count the notebook prints. Tiny specks along edges are not counted.

Why a big sr runs faster
The widest color radius is the quickest, and the saving comes from the pyramid. By default (maxLevel=1) OpenCV first filters a half-size copy, then refines at full size, and that refinement gets cheaper as sr grows: one step costs 0.51, 0.21 and 0.06 seconds at sr 10, 40 and 80 here. With maxLevel=0 the same single step costs 0.78, 0.82 and 0.72 seconds whatever sr is. A wider spatial radius always costs more, because every window covers an area that grows as sp squared.

    
What the result is
The output is a smoothed photo, not a list of segments. Surfaces flatten into near-uniform patches while edges between them stay sharp, which is what makes mean shift filtering useful before thresholding or edge detection. Turning it into segments takes one more step: labeling the connected regions of equal color.

    
Where the numbers come from
Every image and number on this page is precomputed: cv.pyrMeanShiftFiltering was run in the course's cv environment on a 512 by 384 copy of the photo for each of the 40 combinations. Times are wall-clock seconds on one laptop and are only comparable with each other.
